title: Fixing the wait: a needs-first plan for children’s mental health
label: 14 October 2026 · Children and Young People’s Mental Health
summary: Professors Peter Fonagy and Gillian Baird—chair and vice‑chair of the Independent Review into Mental Health Conditions, ADHD and Autism—gave evidence to the Health & Social Care and Education Committees. They argued for a major shift from diagnosis‑first to needs‑first care, earlier support and integrated local services across health, education and welfare. They warned about the harms of long waits, explained drivers of rising need, called for better data and regulation of private assessments, and urged investment in school‑based teams and neighbourhood hubs.

glossary.definition: Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services, specialist NHS mental health care for children and young people.
Education, Health and Care Plan: a legal plan in England describing a child’s special educational needs and support.
Integrated Care Board: local NHS body responsible for planning and funding health services.
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, which issues evidence‑based clinical guidance in England.
A policy allowing families to pay for private assessment when NHS waits are long, while keeping NHS care options.
Pathological Demand Avoidance: a contested clinical profile of demand‑avoidant behaviour that some clinicians link to autism.
Special Educational Needs and Disabilities, the education system term for children needing extra support.
Welfare payments (Personal Independence Payment / Disability Living Allowance) that some families get for disability-related costs.

chapters.title: Purpose and expertise
chapters.takeaway: The reviewers explained their backgrounds and why they were asked to run the independent review.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Professor Fonagy and Professor Baird, welcome. To start: why you were chosen for the review and your relevant experience?

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: I'm a clinical psychologist with four decades in child mental health and have advised NHS England since 2011. That experience made me a natural choice to chair the review.

turns.speaker: Professor Baird
turns.text: I'm a paediatrician specialising in neurodisability, previously a consultant at Guy's and St Thomas'. I co‑chaired the review and have worked on guidelines and research relevant to ADHD, autism and related conditions.

chapters.title: A needs‑first model: top recommendations
chapters.takeaway: They want a system that responds to a child's needs immediately, integrates assessments, focuses on prevention, and strengthens specialist care.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Briefly, what are your top recommendations and which are easiest to implement?

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: We propose a shift from a diagnosis‑first system to a needs‑first system: identify and support needs as soon as a child presents, then prioritise diagnostic work if required.

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: We also want stronger prevention, public‑health approaches to wellbeing, and integrated assessments because neurodevelopmental and mental health problems often co‑occur.

turns.speaker: Professor Baird
turns.text: Integration is crucial. Right now, separate pathways force multiple assessments and long waits. Better integration will reduce duplication and speed support.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You stress that specialist services must be protected, not downgraded.

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: Exactly. Specialist assessment and treatment remain essential; the system just needs to start by addressing need immediately.

chapters.title: Why need is rising: social drivers
chapters.takeaway: Reviewers reject the 'snowflake' idea and point to increased stress, less social support, social media and covid impacts as real drivers.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: Some say today's young people are just less resilient. You reject that—why?

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: Calling them 'snowflakes' is insulting. Evidence shows more stress—financial insecurity, relentless social comparisons on social media, educational pressure—and less local youth provision since 2011.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: How much do factors like social media and sleep each contribute? Where should government focus?

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: They interact, so it's hard to quantify. But social media often displaces protective activities—sleep, exercise, face‑to‑face friendships. Policy should restore protective environments and encourage good habits.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: Would delaying smartphone ownership help?

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: Social norms matter more than bans. Practical parental guidance and creating alternatives—outdoor education, clubs—will be far more effective.

chapters.title: Diagnosis, misdiagnosis and the data gap
chapters.takeaway: They found no evidence of large‑scale overdiagnosis but warned of misdiagnosis, data gaps since 2017, and the risks of long waits.

turns.speaker: Gregory Stafford
turns.text: If environment changes, could someone predisposed to ADHD not become disabled by it? Is it a continuum?

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: Yes—it’s a continuum. ADHD is about attention regulation interacting with environment. Stressful settings make traits more disabling; early support can change outcomes.

turns.speaker: Joe Robertson
turns.text: Your report gives a 1.2% autism population prevalence but >4% diagnosed. Isn't that overdiagnosis?

turns.speaker: Professor Baird
turns.text: We found no evidence of widespread overdiagnosis. Two points: we lack a recent population prevalence study in England (last comprehensive data is from 2017), and diagnostic understanding and thresholds have changed. So administrative diagnosis rates may not reflect 'overdiagnosis' of people with no problems.

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: Overdiagnosis implies there is nothing wrong with people given labels. We see misdiagnosis and changing prevalence signals, but not proof that many people are wrongly labelled and have no need.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What must government do now to fill the evidence gap?

turns.speaker: Professor Baird
turns.text: Commission regular, up‑to‑date population prevalence studies and fund routine data collection so we can track change and evaluate reforms.

chapters.title: Services, schools and parents
chapters.takeaway: They recommended integrated local neighbourhood hubs, better‑resourced school mental health teams, shared language between health and education, and regulating private assessments.

turns.speaker: Josh Fenton-Glynn
turns.text: Parents seek private assessments because waits are so long. Does your model make that irrelevant?

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: We don't recommend abolishing Right to Choose but prioritising NHS needs‑based support would reduce the incentive for expensive private assessments that don't always lead to follow‑up support.

turns.speaker: Josh Fenton-Glynn
turns.text: Should private providers be regulated?

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: Yes. Assessments that NHS pays for should be quality‑regulated—NICE standards and CQC oversight—so assessment equals useful next steps, not just a label.

turns.speaker: Darren Paffey
turns.text: If we move to support‑first, what does that support look like?

turns.speaker: Professor Baird
turns.text: It must be evidence‑based, often psychosocial approaches, delivered earlier in school and community settings, and backed by NICE guidance. It can't be piecemeal or token online courses.

turns.speaker: Jodie Gosling
turns.text: Could needs‑first weaken access to statutory entitlements?

turns.speaker: Professor Baird
turns.text: Safeguards are necessary: integrated local services, clear prioritisation for complexity and risk, and parental confidence-building so diagnosis doesn't become the only route to support.

turns.speaker: Sureena Brackenridge
turns.text: What role should schools play in early identification?

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: Schools are vital: young people rate family, friends and school as top supports. Mental health support teams should be empowered to cover the 'missing middle'—children who need more than basic support but less than specialist CAMHS.

turns.speaker: Professor Baird
turns.text: We back neighbourhood hubs co‑locating health, education and family support, and local commissioning that brings health into planning and action at school level.

turns.speaker: Jen Craft
turns.text: Would placing a legal duty on ICBs to deliver aspects of EHCP help?

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: Yes. Health needs to be at the table and accountable—commissioning for outcomes like participation, not merely processes or diagnoses.

chapters.title: Workforce, digital tools and the single priority
chapters.takeaway: They urged better training for school‑team clinicians, cautious use of digital/AI (clinician remains central), and their single top ask: join up services around children's needs.

turns.speaker: Helen Hayes
turns.text: Mental health support teams need higher expertise. What workforce changes do you recommend?

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: Train teams in proven therapies—CBT, trauma and eating‑disorder interventions—and boost capacity to treat the 'missing middle' rather than only mild cases.

turns.speaker: Professor Baird
turns.text: Co‑location and integrated commissioning would let teams access specialist advice quickly and stop families being pushed between services.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You mention digital assessments and AI; can you point to practical examples?

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: Digital tools can give parents better information and help triage need. But: AI should describe and clinicians decide. There are pilot examples in parts of south London and Scotland, but national scale‑up needs careful testing and standards.

turns.speaker: Professor Baird
turns.text: Digital must be integrated with local services so advice leads to accessible help—not just signposting to commercial sites.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If you had to pick one recommendation for these Committees to press, what would it be?

turns.speaker: Professor Fonagy
turns.text: Bring services together around children's and families' needs—integrated neighbourhood hubs, shared language, joint commissioning and enough resources to respond early.

turns.speaker: Professor Baird
turns.text: I completely agree.
